data.title: AirAsia delays staff salary payments to end of month, internal email shows
data.description: HONG KONG/KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 27 : AirAsia has told employees it will delay salary payments to the end of each month from November through March, according to an internal email seen by Reuters, as the airline takes measures to conserve cash and its Philippine unit cuts jobs. The email, sent to Malaysia-based staff late last week by Chief People Officer Muhammad Khurram Zia, cited the need for a "temporary operational adjustment" at Southeast Asia's largest budget airline, which like its peers faces higher jet fuel costs. Salary payments during the five-month period would be made on the 30th of each month or the last day of February, the email said. It cited a "challenging environment" and asked employees for "patience and flexibility." The email's contents were confirmed by two people familiar with the matter. One of the people said AirAsia had previously paid salaries earlier in the second half of each month. AirAsia did not respond to a request for comment.  The Iran war has sent jet fuel prices soaring, putting airlines worldwide under their worst financial strain since the COVID-19 pandemic. US low-cost carrier Spirit Airlines collapsed in May, Latvia's airBaltic sought bankruptcy protection in September and Norway's Norse Atlantic suspended flights on Thursday as it looks for urgent short-term financing. AIRASIA PHILIPPINES ANNOUNCES LAYOFFS Shares in AirAsia, which employs about 26,000 people predominantly in Asia, have declined more than 70 per cent this year as elevated fuel prices and foreign exchange losses squeezed its operations. AirAsia Philippines said on Thursday it would reduce its workforce following sustained pressure on its operating costs, without specifying how many staff would be affected. The airline said on Friday it remained fully operational and committed to serving the Philippine market. The planned workforce adjustment will not affect passenger flights, booking or other services, AirAsia Philippines General Manager and President Anna Victoria Lu said in a statement. The AirAsia Philippines Pilots' Union filed notice of a strike after 90 pilots were retrenched, its president said in a video posted on social media on Thursday. Philippine Labor Secretary Francis Tolentino confirmed receiving notice in a text message to Reuters. AirAsia reported its third consecutive quarterly loss on Monday, though it was narrower than the prior quarter. Its cash and bank balances stood at 905 million ringgit ($219.93 million) as of September 30, down 5 per cent from June 30.  In an investor presentation accompanying its results, the airline said it was taking measures to conserve cash, including suspending unviable routes and returning 25 planes to lessors.  It said more planes could exit its fleet in 2027, and a creditor restructuring was underway as part of a plan to reset the business before rebuilding in 2028. AirAsia CEO Bo Lingam said on Monday that the third-quarter results suggested "the worst is behind us," while cautioning that fourth-quarter fuel costs were expected to rise further. Malaysia's government has been weighing options to support AirAsia without putting public funds at risk, Reuters has previously reported.  The country's finance ministry said on Thursday that it would ask AirAsia for priority over other lenders and strengthen oversight of the airline's board and management if it decided to extend support. ($1 = 4.1150 ringgit)

data.title: Dollar lingers near 22-month peak as AI worries simmer; kiwi rises
data.description: TOKYO, Nov 27 : The US dollar hovered below a 22-month peak in holiday-thinned trading on Friday, with traders looking to equity markets for clues on direction as doubts about the AI trade trigger heightened volatility. The New Zealand dollar rose after long-awaited results of the general election reduced political uncertainty, even with no clear winner. The Aussie dollar was also pulled higher by its neighbour. The dollar index, which measures the currency against a basket of six peers, was steady at 103.74, at the end of a week that saw it pop to the highest level since March of last year at 104.53 on Monday only to erase those gains a day later. For the week, the index is currently down 0.1 per cent. The US currency was steady at 159.27 yen midway into Friday's Asian session, and has been pinned below 160 yen by worries of another round of Japanese intervention. The greenback weakened 0.1 per cent to 0.83435 Swiss franc. The euro was little changed at $1.09725 and sterling gained slightly to $1.3118. "All eyes are on whether the downtrend in AI-related stocks will turn around," Mizuho analysts wrote in a client note. A recovery could see currencies such as the Aussie and high-yielding Mexican peso bounce back, while renewed selling would likely see those currencies under additional pressure, they said. Japan's tech-heavy Nikkei share index gained 2 per cent on Friday, while South Korea's KOSPI climbed 3.9 per cent. The risk-sensitive Aussie dollar added 0.4 per cent to $0.66635, finding its feet after dipping to a one-year low of $0.6559 on Wednesday. It also got support from a jump in the kiwi dollar earlier in the session, as results of the general election initially lifted the local currency as much as 0.6 per cent. However, those gains later ebbed, and the currency was last 0.3 per cent higher on the day at $0.5484. New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon will seek the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to keep his ruling centre-right coalition in power after official results on Friday showed he fell just short of a parliamentary majority. "NZD has risen slightly on the reduction — but not removal — of uncertainty, but the move is polluted by the USD effect," said Imre Speizer, Westpac's head of New Zealand market strategy. "Risks of another breakdown remain, and we wouldn't rule out $0.5400 during the week ahead," he said. "Much of the bearish impetus has been due to the surging US dollar and hawkish Fed repricing." The US currency has been supported by expectations for Federal Reserve policy tightening, with traders seeing a quarter-point interest rate hike on December 9 as a near certainty, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool. Hotter-than-expected US core personal consumption expenditures inflation in October, a sharp upward revision to third-quarter gross domestic product and a Federal Reserve survey showing continued economic growth and sticky inflation also have traders confident of an additional hike by around April. The dollar index has risen about 5.7 per cent so far in 2026, with only a month left in the year. The index is up 1.7 per cent this month, putting it on track for its first run of three straight monthly gains since the final three months of 2024. "The USD looks to be on a stronger-for-longer path than previously expected," NAB strategists wrote in a research report. However, "given its rapid rise, we see limited scope for further gains," they added.

data.title: Japan Tobacco shares surge on talk it may acquire part of Imperial
data.description: TOKYO, Nov 27 : Japan Tobacco shares jumped on Friday on the prospect of it joining hands with Altria to acquire and split up British cigarette maker Imperial Brands in a potential multibillion-dollar deal. US tobacco group Altria said a day earlier that it is considering a possible all-cash bid for Imperial Brands and is evaluating an acquisition with a partner which may purchase part of the business. Bloomberg News has also reported JT is evaluating an acquisition with a partner. JT declined to comment on the report. Imperial said it has not received any approach, but would consider any proposal. A deal for Imperial, which owns cigarette brands such as Davidoff, Gauloises and Kool and has a market value of £25.90 billion ($34 billion), is widely viewed as making sense for both JT and Altria. JT, whose brands include Camel, Benson & Hedges and the Ploom heated tobacco device range, has been expanding in the United States, particularly in cheaper labels that have been winning market share. Taking on Imperial's US assets would improve its presence significantly in an attractive market, analysts say. A deal could "turn JT into a sizeable, diversified, and value-rational 3rd-place US competitor with cost synergy potential," Jefferies analyst Andrei Andon-Ionita said in a note to clients. Shares in JT gained 4 per cent in afternoon trade, outperforming a 1.8 per cent gain for Japan's benchmark TOPIX index. JT, which is 37.6 per cent owned by the Japanese government, has also been active in acquiring assets in Africa for more than a decade, including in Ethiopia, Egypt and Sudan. Purchasing Imperial's African and Middle Eastern businesses would dovetail with efforts in Africa so far and could help replace lost revenue after ​President Vladimir Putin ordered the seizure of the company's Russian assets this month. The potential deal reflects mounting pressure on cigarette makers to find new growth as smoking rates fall — a decline that has been difficult to completely offset with newer nicotine products. If completed with a premium to Imperial's current market value, it would mark the third-largest transaction targeting a tobacco company in history, LSEG data shows. It would also be the largest takeover in the sector in a decade, after British American Tobacco acquired US peer Reynolds American Inc for $60 billion including debt in 2016. For Altria, a deal could mark a return to international cigarette sales, two decades after it spun off its international division to focus on the United States. That move created Philip Morris International. Altria has not sold cigarettes or most other products outside the US since, leaving it more exposed than rivals to several key challenges in that market. BTIG analyst Owen Bennett also said in a note to clients that the deal "could be done without impacting the current credit ratings of either name." JT had 887.3 billion yen ($5.6 billion) in cash and cash equivalents at the end of September. It could also help finance the deal by re-issuing non-cancelled treasury shares for roughly $7.4 billion, BTIG's Bennett added. ($1 = 159.2800 yen)

data.title: Tokyo core inflation at 16-month high, bolsters case for BOJ hike
data.description: TOKYO: Annual core inflation in Japan's capital accelerated in November at the fastest pace in 16 months, highlighting mounting price pressure and bolstering the case for an interest rate hike as soon as next month. The data, widely regarded as a leading indicator of nationwide trends, will be among the factors the Bank of Japan scrutinises in deciding whether to raise interest rates at its next two-day policy meeting ending on Dec 18. The core consumer price index, which includes prices of fuel but not fresh food, in Tokyo rose 2.9 per cent in November from a year earlier, data showed on Friday, compared with the median market forecast of 3.0 per cent. It followed a 2.6 per cent gain in October and marked the fastest year-on-year rise since July 2025. Core inflation in Tokyo, which is seen as a leading indicator of nationwide trends, thus stayed above the BOJ's 2 per cent target for three straight months, cementing the case for further hikes. While the increase was driven partly by an end to government utility subsidies, prices rose for a broad range of goods and services including food, daily necessities and hotel charges. "Core consumer inflation is expected to accelerate due to rising energy prices from the Middle East conflict and ensuing second-round effects," said Masato Koike, senior economist at Sompo Institute Plus. "If the current market instability stemming from concern over the AI and chip outlook persists, there's a chance the BOJ may forgo a rate hike in December. But our baseline projection is for the BOJ to proceed with one next month," he said. An index stripping away the effect of volatile fresh food and fuel prices, which is closely watched by the BOJ as a more accurate gauge of trend inflation, rose 2.5 per cent in November after a 2.6 per cent gain in October, the data showed. Inflation rose for services including public transportation and medical care, suggesting the shift in Japan's inflation dynamics is no longer driven only by temporary supply shocks, said Ayako Fujita, chief Japan economist at JPMorgan Securities. "We expect the momentum in price increases to remain broad-based" toward the first quarter of 2027, she said. "While momentum in core goods inflation should gradually ease, we expect inflationary pressures to broaden further across food and services." Short-term Japanese government bond yields edged higher on Friday as signs of persistent inflation reinforced expectations of a rate hike next month. Investors are focusing on what hints BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda could drop on the likelihood of a December rate hike, and the future rate-hike path, in a speech scheduled for Monday. CLOSE TO TERMINAL? With stubbornly high energy costs and rising import costs from a weak yen adding to inflationary pressures, the BOJ raised its policy rate to 1.25 per cent in September after delivering a hike in June - a shorter interval than the roughly twice-a-year hikes seen in 2024 and 2025. The central bank kept rates steady in October, but said underlying inflation has roughly hit its 2 per cent target and signalled its readiness to continue hiking rates to prevent price growth from accelerating too much. A majority of analysts polled by Reuters expect the BOJ to raise rates in December and follow up with another hike by end-March. Many see the terminal rate at around 1.75 per cent or 2.0 per cent. Hawkish BOJ board member Naoki Tamura said on Thursday the central bank must respond swiftly to signs of an inflation overshoot, including by accelerating the pace of rate hikes. While many analysts view two more rate hikes as all but certain, there is less conviction on how far the BOJ can tighten beyond that, with inflationary pressures from higher energy costs and a weak yen expected to ease in the second half of next year. Shigeto Nagai, head of Japan Economics at Oxford Economics, projects headline inflation to slow to 2 per cent in late 2027. "We think this will allow the BOJ to complete its multi-year rate normalisation process by mid-2027, hitting a terminal policy rate of 1.75 per cent," he said.

data.title: Commentary: Black Friday is here, but what’s behind our need to chase bargains?
data.description: CARDIFF: Black Friday is a highly successful US export. The retail strategy designed to kickstart festive shopping has become a global phenomenon. But are the hype and the pressure (and the occasional fight over electrical hardware) worth it? After all, most products on offer during Black Friday are available at the same price (or even less) at other times of the year. So why do so many people still join in? Here are some of the marketing tricks and psychological drivers that help to explain the appeal of Black Friday.  MARKETING PUSH Offers that exist for a limited time period are among the oldest retail marketing tricks in the book. And there is plenty of research which shows that they reliably increase a shopper’s intention to buy. If we think a deal will disappear after Black Friday, the fear of missing out on a bargain can push us towards buying that air fryer or scented candle. Or we might buy it to avoid the potential feelings of regret that may come if we don’t. Price tags also have a big effect. Psychologists have shown that when making value judgments, the first number we see disproportionately shapes how we evaluate subsequent numbers. So when a price tag reads: “"Was £100 (US$131)! Now £60!”, the £100 figure is the one we latch on to. This makes £60 feel like a £40 saving rather than a £60 expense, even if the item was never really worth £100 in the first place. CONSUMER PULL While many people will be aware of these kinds of retail marketing tricks, they will still willingly participate in Black Friday. This may be partly due to its timing, but also to the psychological rewards that shopping could offer. In the northern hemisphere at least, Black Friday coincides with the “winter blues”, potentially offering a source of excitement as the days get colder and darker. We may also shop to improve our mood with a little “retail therapy”.One explanation for the effectiveness of retail therapy is that negative emotions often come from situations we cannot change. Making choices about what we want and then buying those things might help us to restore a feeling of personal control. Another reason is that buying generally might bring more positive than negative emotions. But studies have also shown that the temporary uplift from purchasing does not last as long as we often think it will. Landing a bargain can also make us feel good about ourselves. Being a “smart shopper” has been linked to a personal sense of achievement and pride when we secure a good deal. Buying things at a (genuine) discount can also demonstrate competence and good financial management to others. But that is not the only social appeal of Black Friday. Even the most independently minded consumer can be influenced by what other people do. And engaging in an activity at the same time as others, even among strangers, can temporarily enhance feelings of social connection.WHAT ARE WE REALLY BUYING? Despite the thrill of a bargain, or joining in with a commercial social event, what feels rewarding in the moment may not necessarily contribute to our longer-term wellbeing. Research in consumption has shown that spending money on things that fit our personality or that help us with personal goals might be a good idea. For example, an extrovert or someone looking to develop new connections will probably benefit more from spending money on social activities than buying a discounted item. But why we buy is as important as what we buy. In a recent study, my colleagues and I found that spending money in response to social pressure, to gain status or to seek others’ approval was linked to low wellbeing. So even experiences do not always bring more happiness. Our expectations can also mislead us. In another study I worked on, my colleagues and I found that people thought that buying new clothes would make them feel better about themselves than buying second-hand clothes. But it turned out that buying old and new clothes had pretty much the same effect. More broadly, research shows that focusing on economic gains and consumption brings a lower sense of wellbeing and is detrimental to our personal relationships. In contrast, choosing to live more simply or buying less is consistently linked with greater wellbeing. People who become less focused on material goals tend to become happier over time. So perhaps Black Friday should not simply be about how much money we are saving or how much temporary joy our purchases might bring us. Maybe it’s a time to reflect on what we gain from spending more money on more stuff, and whether there might be more sustainable and lasting alternatives. Olaya Moldes Andres is Senior Lecturer in Consumer Behaviour at Cardiff University. This commentary first appeared on The Conversation.

data.title: Japan's JERA enters talks with Anthropic, Meta to build data centres, Nikkei reports
data.description: Nov 27 : Japan's largest power generator, JERA, has entered into talks with Anthropic, Meta, and other US tech giants to build data centers near power plants in the Tokyo area, the Nikkei newspaper reported on Friday. JERA Global CEO and Chair Yukio Kani said in a recent interview that the energy group is also in discussions with Amazon, Microsoft and Google, Nikkei reported. JERA announced a partnership with Dell Technologies and UK-based AI infrastructure developer RHAELM in October to accelerate the development of artificial intelligence infrastructure in Japan. They signed a memorandum of understanding to develop a standardised model for building AI infrastructure on a national scale, starting with a $15 billion hyperscale data centre in Chiba, near Tokyo. A JERA spokesperson said RHAELM is in charge of marketing and the company had been told that RHAELM is in talks with multiple hyperscalers. RHAELM was not immediately available for comment. Anthropic, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft and Google did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment.

data.title: SAP reportedly considering at least 10,000 job cuts in AI restructuring
data.description: German software giant SAP is considering cutting at least 10,000 jobs in an AI-driven restructuring, Bloomberg News reported on Thursday (Nov 26), citing people familiar with the matter. The restructuring would affect at least 9 per cent of SAP's global workforce, Bloomberg said, adding that the total number of job cuts could change after labour negotiations. SAP, Europe's most valuable tech company, declined to commment. The plans have yet to be discussed with employee representatives, the Financial Times reported, citing people familiar with the matter. SAP joins a growing list of major German companies weighing workforce reductions after automakers including Volkswagen and BMW have announced deep cuts as they grapple with sluggish demand and increasing competition from China, reported Financial Times.  US technology rivals including Microsoft , Oracle and Salesforce have also announced thousands of job cuts in recent months, citing AI-driven efficiencies and efforts to cut costs.  If implemented, the plan would mark SAP's second major round of layoffs in about two years.  The software giant slashed 10,000 jobs in a major restructuring in 2024, though subsequent hiring has pushed its total headcount back up to about 113,000, according to Financial Times.

data.title: Japan Tobacco shares climb on talk that it may be part of Imperial Brands takeover
data.description: TOKYO, Nov 27 : Japan Tobacco shares rose on Friday following a report that it was considering partnering on a multibillion-dollar takeover of British cigarette maker Imperial Brands — potentially one of the largest in the industry's history. A day earlier, US tobacco group Altria said it was considering a possible all-cash bid for Imperial Brands and was discussing a deal involving acquiring part of its business with another party. Tokyo-based JT is considering teaming up with a partner, Bloomberg News reported. JT declined to comment on the report. In morning trade, JT shares were up 3.6 per cent, outperforming a 1 per cent gain for Japan's benchmark TOPIX index. The potential deal reflects mounting pressure on cigarette makers to find new growth avenues as smoking rates fall — a decline that has been difficult to completely offset with newer nicotine products. Shares in Imperial, which said it had not received an approach but whose board would consider any proposal, jumped 13.8 per cent on Thursday, valuing it at £25.90 billion ($34 billion). Imperial would give a buyer a portfolio of established cigarette brands including Davidoff, Gauloises and Kool, which are sold in more than 100 markets. "This deal would make a lot of sense for both (Altria) and JT, in our view, while we believe the deal could be done without impacting the current credit ratings of either name," BTIG analyst Owen Bennett said in a note. JT, whose brands include Camel, Benson & Hedges and the Ploom heated tobacco device range, could acquire assets from Imperial Brands in the US, Africa and the Middle East, Bennett said. JT has been expanding its US tobacco business, particularly in cheaper labels that have been winning market share. A deal could "turn JT into a sizeable, diversified, and value-rational 3rd-place US competitor with cost synergy potential," Jefferies analyst Andrei Andon-Ionita said in a note. A takeover by JT of Imperial's US business should avoid antitrust issues given a combined value share of 14 per cent, smaller than Altria and British American Tobacco, he said. In recent years, JT has done deals in countries such as Bangladesh, the Philippines and Ethiopia. JT, whose shareholders include the Japanese government, said last week it would record an $8.7 billion loss after losing control of its Russian subsidiaries when ​President Vladimir Putin ordered their seizure this month. That seizure will continue to impede any share gains for Japan Tobacco, said Tatsunori Kawai, chief strategist at Mitsubishi UFJ eSmart Securities.

data.title: BOJ calls for safeguards against digital money, AI risks
data.description: TOKYO, Nov 27 : Global policymakers must strengthen defences against financial stability and cybersecurity risks posed by the emergence of new forms of digital money and financial infrastructure, Bank of Japan Executive Director Kazushige Kamiyama said on Friday. New forms of digital money, such as stablecoins and tokenised deposits, are likely to co-exist and interact, which poses fresh challenges for policymakers such as ensuring the diversity does not create unnecessary fragmentation or undermine financial stability, he said. The growing use of AI also brings fresh cybersecurity risks, requiring authorities and institutions to strengthen their defences against the growing ability of AI to discover and exploit vulnerabilities, Kamiyama said. "My central message is that technological innovation offers significant opportunities to improve money and payments, but innovation must go hand in hand with trust," Kamiyama said in a speech delivered to the International Monetary Fund's seminar on digital money and payments in Tokyo. "Central bank money will continue to play a fundamental role as the anchor of trust in the monetary system," he said.

data.title: Chinese industrial profit rises 16% in January-October
data.description: BEIJING, Nov 27 : Profit at Chinese industrial firms rose 16 per cent in the first 10 months of this year over the corresponding period last year, official data showed on Friday. The increase quickened from 15.5 per cent in the January-September period, showed data from the National Bureau of Statistics. Industrial profit figures cover firms with annual revenue of at least 20 million yuan ($3 million) from main operations. ($1 = 6.6722 Chinese yuan)
